--- title: "Testing your code" page-layout: article jupyter: julia-1.12 --- Up to now, we have checked our functions by calling them and looking at what is printed: `println(convert_temperature(100, unit="C")) # Outputs: 212.0`. This is already a test, but a fragile one: *you* have to read the output, compare it with the expected value, and redo it by hand every time the code changes. In this page, you will learn to write **automated tests**: small pieces of code that check that your functions behave as expected, and that you can run again in one command after each modification. Tests are useful to: - **find bugs** early, while the code is still fresh in your mind; - **modify code without fear**: if you break something, a test will tell you; - **document** how a function is supposed to be used, with concrete examples. ## The `Test` standard library Julia ships with the [`Test`](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/stdlib/Test/) standard library: there is nothing to install, just load it. ::: {#1d06c292 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Test ``` ::: ### The `@test` macro The macro `@test` evaluates an expression that must return `true` or `false`. If the result is `true`, the test **passes**. ::: {#3af2b3d5 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.julia .cell-code} @test 1 + 1 == 2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
Test Passed
``` ::: ::: ::: If the result is `false`, the test **fails** and Julia reports both sides of the comparison, which helps to understand what went wrong. ::: {#0914c40e .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.julia .cell-code} try #| hide_line @test 1 + 1 == 3 catch end #| hide_line ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Test Failed at In[5]:2 Expression: 1 + 1 == 3 Evaluated: 2 == 3 ``` ::: ::: ### Comparing floating-point numbers Floating-point numbers are stored with a finite precision (see the page on [types](types.qmd)), so exact comparisons can fail even when the mathematics is correct: ::: {#b5bcc650 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.julia .cell-code} try #| hide_line @test 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 catch end #| hide_line ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Test Failed at In[6]:2 Expression: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 Evaluated: 0.30000000000000004 == 0.3 ``` ::: ::: To compare floating-point numbers, use the approximate comparison `≈` (type `\approx` then `Tab`), which is the function `isapprox`. You can control the tolerance with the keyword arguments `atol` (absolute tolerance) and `rtol` (relative tolerance). ::: {#29d457c2 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.julia .cell-code} @test 0.1 + 0.2 ≈ 0.3 @test π ≈ 3.14 atol = 1e-2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
Test Passed
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} By default, `≈` uses only a relative tolerance. Therefore `x ≈ 0` is `true` only if `x == 0`! When the expected value is zero, always give an absolute tolerance: `@test x ≈ 0 atol = 1e-10`. ::: ### Testing errors with `@test_throws` A function must also behave correctly when it receives invalid inputs. Recall the function `convert_temperature` from the page [Structure your code](structure.qmd), which throws an `ArgumentError` for an unknown unit: ::: {#8919eb48 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function convert_temperature(value; unit) if unit == "C" return value * 9/5 + 32 elseif unit == "F" return (value - 32) * 5/9 else throw(ArgumentError("Unit must be 'C' or 'F'")) end end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` convert_temperature (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: The macro `@test_throws` checks that an expression throws an exception of the given type: ::: {#50ac6a2e .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.julia .cell-code} @test_throws ArgumentError convert_temperature(10, unit="K") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
Test Passed
      Thrown: ArgumentError
``` ::: ::: ::: ### Grouping tests with `@testset` Tests are grouped into **test sets**. A test set runs all its tests, even if some of them fail, and prints a summary at the end. Test sets can be nested. ::: {#56fffc65 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.julia .cell-code} @testset "convert_temperature" begin @testset "Celsius to Fahrenheit" begin @test convert_temperature(100, unit="C") ≈ 212 @test convert_temperature(0, unit="C") ≈ 32 end @testset "Fahrenheit to Celsius" begin @test convert_temperature(32, unit="F") ≈ 0 atol = 1e-12 end @testset "invalid unit" begin @test_throws ArgumentError convert_temperature(10, unit="K") end end; ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Test Summary: | Pass Total Time convert_temperature | 4 4 0.0s ``` ::: ::: When at least one test fails, the summary shows where, and an error is raised at the end of the test set: ::: {#b1e3f148 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.julia .cell-code} try #| hide_line @testset "a test set with a failure" begin @test 2 * 3 == 6 @test 2 + 3 == 6 @test 2 - 3 == -1 end; catch end #| hide_line ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a test set with a failure: Test Failed at In[11]:4 Expression: 2 + 3 == 6 Evaluated: 5 == 6 Stacktrace: [1] top-level scope @ In[11]:3 [2] macro expansion @ ~/.julia/juliaup/julia-1.12.6+0.aarch64.apple.darwin14/Julia-1.12.app/Contents/Resources/julia/share/julia/stdlib/v1.12/Test/src/Test.jl:1777 [inlined] [3] macro expansion @ In[11]:4 [inlined] [4] macro expansion @ ~/.julia/juliaup/julia-1.12.6+0.aarch64.apple.darwin14/Julia-1.12.app/Contents/Resources/julia/share/julia/stdlib/v1.12/Test/src/Test.jl:680 [inlined] Test Summary: | Pass Fail Total Time a test set with a failure | 2 1 3 1.3s RNG of the outermost testset: Random.Xoshiro(0x96bc558eabebde3c, 0xea2d2416166db562, 0x4fee37d687f81709, 0x4865ec1902b74b1a, 0xdfb44db0aa107f45) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Test sets and loops A `@testset` can be combined with a `for` loop to run the same tests on several inputs. Each iteration is reported separately. ::: {#183dab06 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.julia .cell-code} @testset "round trip for T = $T" for T in (Float32, Float64) x = T(37) @test convert_temperature(convert_temperature(x, unit="C"), unit="F") ≈ x end; ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Test Summary: | Pass Total Time round trip for T = Float32 | 1 1 0.0s Test Summary: | Pass Total Time round trip for T = Float64 | 1 1 0.0s ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Other useful macros | Macro | Usage | |-------|-------| | `@test ex` | `ex` must return `true`. | | `@test a ≈ b atol=...` | approximate comparison. | | `@test_throws T ex` | `ex` must throw an exception of type `T`. | | `@testset "name" begin ... end` | groups tests and prints a summary. | | `@test_broken ex` | documents a *known* bug: the test is expected to fail. | | `@inferred f(x)` | checks that the return type of `f(x)` is inferred by the compiler (see [type stability](performance.qmd)). | ## What should I test? The contract of a function Before writing tests, you need to know precisely **what the function is supposed to do**. This specification is called the **contract** of the function, and the right place to write it is the [docstring](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1/manual/documentation/), just above the function. A contract states: - the **preconditions**: what the inputs must satisfy; - the **postconditions**: what the function returns (or modifies) when the preconditions hold; - what happens when the preconditions are **not** satisfied (typically, which error is thrown). ```julia """ my_mean(v) Return the arithmetic mean of the vector `v`. - Precondition: `v` is a non-empty vector of real numbers. - Postcondition: returns `sum(v) / length(v)`; `v` is not modified. - Throws an `ArgumentError` if `v` is empty. """ ``` Once the contract is written, a good test suite covers: 1. **typical cases**: a few "normal" inputs for which you know the answer (computed by hand); 2. **edge cases**: the smallest inputs (empty vector, one element), the values *exactly* at a boundary (if a condition reads `x >= 10`, test `9`, `10` and `11`), zeros, negative numbers...; 3. **invalid inputs**: one `@test_throws` per error described in the contract; 4. **properties**: relations that must always hold, even if you do not know the exact result (a converted temperature converted back gives the initial value, the output of a sort is sorted, the input is not modified...). ::: {.callout-important} A test that is never red is useless. When you write a test, check that it is able to fail: temporarily break the code and verify that the test detects it. ::: ## Organising tests in a package In a notebook or in the REPL, you can write tests anywhere. In a real project, the code lives in a **package** and the tests in a separate folder, so that anyone can run them with a single command. Creating a package takes one line in the package mode of the REPL (see [Developer set up](developer_setup.qmd)): ```julia ] generate MyStats ``` Then add the folder `test` with a file `runtests.jl`, so that your project looks like this: ``` MyStats/ ├── Project.toml ├── src/ │ └── MyStats.jl # the code: module MyStats ... end └── test/ └── runtests.jl # the tests ``` The file `src/MyStats.jl` contains the module (see [Modules](structure.qmd#modules)): ```julia module MyStats export my_mean """ my_mean(v) Return the arithmetic mean of the non-empty vector `v`. Throw an `ArgumentError` if `v` is empty. """ function my_mean(v) if isempty(v) throw(ArgumentError("v must be non-empty")) end return sum(v) / length(v) end end ``` The file `test/runtests.jl` loads the package and runs the tests: ```julia using MyStats using Test @testset "MyStats" begin @test my_mean([1, 2, 3]) == 2 @test my_mean([1.0, 2.0]) ≈ 1.5 end ``` Finally, declare `Test` as a dependency used *only for testing* by adding these lines at the end of `Project.toml`: ```toml [extras] Test = "8dfed614-e22c-5e08-85e1-65c5234f0b40" [targets] test = ["Test"] ``` ### Running the tests From the folder `MyStats`, start Julia, activate the package and run its tests: ```julia ] activate . ] test ``` ``` Testing Running tests... Test Summary: | Pass Total Time MyStats | 2 2 0.0s Testing MyStats tests passed ``` ### Code coverage All tests pass... but is all the code tested? The **code coverage** measures which lines of your code have been executed by the tests. The package [LocalCoverage.jl](https://github.com/JuliaCI/LocalCoverage.jl) runs the tests and prints a report. Install it once in your *global* environment (not in the package): ```julia ] activate ] add LocalCoverage ``` Then, from the folder containing `MyStats`: ```julia using LocalCoverage cov = generate_coverage("MyStats") # runs the tests with coverage show(IOContext(stdout, :print_gaps => true), cov) # also print the missed lines ``` ``` ┌────────────────┬───────┬─────┬──────┬─────┬──────┐ │ Filename │ Lines │ Hit │ Miss │ % │ Gaps │ ├────────────────┼───────┼─────┼──────┼─────┼──────┤ │ src/MyStats.jl │ 4 │ 3 │ 1 │ 75% │ 13 │ ├────────────────┼───────┼─────┼──────┼─────┼──────┤ │ TOTAL │ 4 │ 3 │ 1 │ 75% │ │ └────────────────┴───────┴─────┴──────┴─────┴──────┘ ``` Line 13, `throw(ArgumentError(...))`, is never executed: we forgot to test the empty vector. Adding `@test_throws ArgumentError my_mean(Int[])` to the tests brings the coverage to 100%. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Coverage is a tool, not a goal A line that is **executed** is not necessarily **verified**: `my_mean([1, 2, 3])` executes every line of a wrong implementation as well. Moreover, coverage cannot see code that is *missing* (a forgotten `if`). A coverage of 100% does not mean that the code is correct; a low coverage, however, tells you for sure that some parts of the code are not tested. ::: ::: {.callout-note} In the package directory, `] test` can also be run from a terminal with `julia --project -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.test()'`. This is what continuous integration services (for instance GitHub Actions) do after each modification of the code. ::: ## Exercises For each exercise, work in a script or in the REPL, after `using Test`. ### Exercise 1: Your first test set Consider the function `convert_temperature` defined above. 1. Write a test set `"convert_temperature"` containing at least: - two typical conversions from Celsius to Fahrenheit and two from Fahrenheit to Celsius (compute the expected values by hand); - the particular value $-40$, which is the same in both units; - a test checking that an invalid unit throws an `ArgumentError`. 2. Add a **property** test: for several values `x` (use a `for` loop), converting `x` from Celsius to Fahrenheit and back gives `x`. 3. Check that your tests are able to fail: replace `9/5` by `9/4` in the function, run the tests again and look at the report. Do not forget to restore the function! ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon=false} ## Hint for Exercise 1 Remember to use `≈` and not `==` when comparing floating-point numbers. When the expected value is `0`, you need an absolute tolerance `atol`. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false} ## Correction of Exercise 1 ::: {#e785d4ce .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.julia .cell-code} @testset "convert_temperature" begin @testset "Celsius to Fahrenheit" begin @test convert_temperature(0, unit="C") ≈ 32 @test convert_temperature(100, unit="C") ≈ 212 end @testset "Fahrenheit to Celsius" begin @test convert_temperature(212, unit="F") ≈ 100 @test convert_temperature(32, unit="F") ≈ 0 atol = 1e-12 end @testset "-40 is the same in both units" begin @test convert_temperature(-40, unit="C") ≈ -40 @test convert_temperature(-40, unit="F") ≈ -40 end @testset "invalid unit" begin @test_throws ArgumentError convert_temperature(10, unit="K") @test_throws ArgumentError convert_temperature(10, unit="c") # case matters end @testset "round trip" begin for x in (-273.15, -10.5, 0.0, 37.2, 1000.0) @test convert_temperature(convert_temperature(x, unit="C"), unit="F") ≈ x end end end; ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Test Summary: | Pass Total Time convert_temperature | 13 13 0.0s ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Exercise 2: Catch the bugs with your tests We want a function computing the median of a vector. Here is its contract: ```julia """ median(v) Return the median of the vector `v`. - Precondition: `v` is a non-empty vector of real numbers (not necessarily sorted). - Postcondition: if `length(v)` is odd, returns the middle value of the sorted vector; if `length(v)` is even, returns the mean of the two middle values of the sorted vector. The vector `v` is not modified. - Throws an `ArgumentError` if `v` is empty. """ ``` Six students have written an implementation, named `median_1`, ..., `median_6`: only **one** of them respects the contract. 1. **Without reading the implementations**, write a function `test_median(median)` which takes an implementation as argument and runs a `@testset` checking the contract. 2. Run `test_median` on the six implementations given below. A good test suite must **fail** for the five wrong implementations and **pass** for the correct one. How many bugs did you catch? 3. If some wrong implementations pass your tests, read their code, find the bug, and add the missing tests. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false} ## The six implementations (to copy in your script) ::: {#629ddc4a .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function median_1(v) isempty(v) && throw(ArgumentError("v must be non-empty")) s = sort!(v) n = length(s) return isodd(n) ? s[(n + 1) ÷ 2] : (s[n ÷ 2] + s[n ÷ 2 + 1]) / 2 end function median_2(v) isempty(v) && throw(ArgumentError("v must be non-empty")) s = v n = length(s) return isodd(n) ? s[(n + 1) ÷ 2] : (s[n ÷ 2] + s[n ÷ 2 + 1]) / 2 end function median_3(v) isempty(v) && throw(ArgumentError("v must be non-empty")) s = sort(v) n = length(s) return isodd(n) ? s[(n + 1) ÷ 2] : s[n ÷ 2] end function median_4(v) isempty(v) && throw(ArgumentError("v must be non-empty")) s = sort(v) n = length(s) return isodd(n) ? s[(n + 1) ÷ 2] : (s[n ÷ 2] + s[n ÷ 2 + 1]) / 2 end function median_5(v) s = sort(v) n = length(s) return isodd(n) ? s[(n + 1) ÷ 2] : (s[n ÷ 2] + s[n ÷ 2 + 1]) / 2 end function median_6(v) isempty(v) && throw(ArgumentError("v must be non-empty")) s = sort(v) n = length(s) return isodd(n) ? s[(n + 1) ÷ 2] : (s[n ÷ 2] + s[n ÷ 2 + 1]) ÷ 2 end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` median_6 (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon=false} ## Hint for Exercise 2 In Julia, functions are values: they can be passed as arguments to other functions. Inside `test_median`, call `median(...)` as usual, it refers to the argument. Then, for each item of the contract, ask yourself: *which input would reveal that this item is not respected?* Think about vectors of odd **and** even length, **unsorted** vectors, integer inputs whose median is not an integer, and the empty vector. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false} ## Correction of Exercise 2 Each test set targets one item of the contract: ::: {#2a94a134 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function test_median(median) @testset "$median" begin @testset "odd length" begin @test median([3]) == 3 @test median([3, 1, 2]) == 2 # unsorted input end @testset "even length" begin @test median([1, 2]) == 1.5 # the median is not an integer @test median([4, 1, 3, 2]) == 2.5 # unsorted input end @testset "input is not modified" begin v = [3, 1, 2] median(v) @test v == [3, 1, 2] end @testset "empty input" begin @test_throws ArgumentError median(Int[]) end end end; ``` ::: We run it on the six implementations. The output of the tests is hidden with `@suppress` from the package `Suppressor`, and we only print whether the implementation passes the tests: ::: {#8e15ff0e .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Suppressor for median in (median_1, median_2, median_3, median_4, median_5, median_6) passed = try @suppress test_median(median) true catch false end println(median, passed ? ": passes the tests" : ": bug caught!") end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` median_1: bug caught! median_2: bug caught! median_3: bug caught! median_4: passes the tests median_5: bug caught! median_6: bug caught! ``` ::: ::: The bugs were: - `median_1` uses `sort!`, which **modifies** the input vector; - `median_2` does **not sort** the vector; - `median_3` returns the lower middle value when the length is even; - `median_4` is correct; - `median_5` throws a `BoundsError` instead of an `ArgumentError` for an empty vector; - `median_6` uses the integer division `÷`: `median_6([1, 2])` returns `1` instead of `1.5`. ::: ### Exercise 3: The tests are red, fix the code The [bisection method](root_finding.qmd) finds a root of a continuous function $f$ on an interval $[a, b]$ such that $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ have opposite signs, by halving the interval repeatedly. Here is a first implementation, with its contract: ```julia """ bisection(f, a, b; tol=1e-12, max_iter=100) Find a root of the continuous function `f` in the interval `[a, b]`. - Preconditions: `a < b` and `f(a) * f(b) ≤ 0`. - Postcondition: returns a tuple `(x, iter)` where `x` is an approximation of a root of `f` in `[a, b]` and `iter` is the number of iterations. If `f(a) == 0` (resp. `f(b) == 0`), then `x == a` (resp. `x == b`). - Throws an `ArgumentError` if a precondition is not satisfied. """ function bisection(f, a, b; tol=1e-12, max_iter=100) if f(a) * f(b) > 0 error("The function must have opposite signs at the endpoints a and b.") end mid = (a + b) / 2 iter_count = 0 while (b - a) / 2 > tol && iter_count < max_iter iter_count += 1 mid = (a + b) / 2 if abs(f(mid)) ≤ tol return mid, iter_count elseif f(a) * f(mid) < 0 b = mid else a = mid end end return mid, iter_count end ``` Here are the tests of this function: ```julia @testset "bisection" begin @testset "typical cases" begin x, _ = bisection(x -> cos(x) - x, 0, 1) @test x ≈ 0.7390851332151607 atol = 1e-10 x, _ = bisection(x -> x^2 - 2, 0, 2) @test x ≈ sqrt(2) atol = 1e-10 x, _ = bisection(x -> 1 - x, 0, 2) # f is decreasing @test x ≈ 1 atol = 1e-10 end @testset "root at an endpoint" begin @test bisection(x -> x, 0.0, 1.0)[1] == 0.0 @test bisection(x -> x - 1, 0.0, 1.0)[1] == 1.0 end @testset "invalid inputs" begin @test_throws ArgumentError bisection(x -> x^2 + 1, 0.0, 1.0) # no sign change @test_throws ArgumentError bisection(x -> x, 1.0, -1.0) # a > b end end ``` 1. Run the tests. Which ones fail? For each failing test, read the report and explain **why** the code does not respect its contract. 2. Fix the function until all the tests pass. You must not modify the tests! 3. *Bonus*: the function `f` is evaluated several times at the same point. Modify the code so that each iteration evaluates `f` only once, and check that the tests still pass. This is the main interest of tests: you can improve the code safely. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon=false} ## Hint for Exercise 3 Four tests fail. Look at what happens in the loop when `f(a) == 0`: what is the value of `f(a) * f(mid)`? Also, which type of exception does the function `error` throw? ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false} ## Correction of Exercise 3 The failing tests are: - `bisection(x -> x, 0.0, 1.0)`: since `f(a) == 0`, the product `f(a) * f(mid)` is always `0`, so the code always executes `a = mid` and moves away from the root. It returns a value close to `1` instead of `0`. - `bisection(x -> x - 1, 0.0, 1.0)`: the method converges to `1` but never returns exactly `b`. - `bisection(x -> x^2 + 1, 0.0, 1.0)`: `error(...)` throws an `ErrorException`, not an `ArgumentError`. - `bisection(x -> x, 1.0, -1.0)`: the condition `a < b` is never checked. The loop is not executed and the function returns silently. A corrected version, which also evaluates `f` only once per iteration: ::: {#923f833b .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function bisection(f, a, b; tol=1e-12, max_iter=100) a < b || throw(ArgumentError("a must be smaller than b")) fa, fb = f(a), f(b) fa == 0 && return a, 0 fb == 0 && return b, 0 fa * fb < 0 || throw(ArgumentError("f(a) and f(b) must have opposite signs")) mid = (a + b) / 2 iter_count = 0 while (b - a) / 2 > tol && iter_count < max_iter iter_count += 1 mid = (a + b) / 2 fmid = f(mid) if abs(fmid) ≤ tol return mid, iter_count elseif fa * fmid < 0 b = mid else a, fa = mid, fmid end end return mid, iter_count end @testset "bisection" begin @testset "typical cases" begin x, _ = bisection(x -> cos(x) - x, 0, 1) @test x ≈ 0.7390851332151607 atol = 1e-10 x, _ = bisection(x -> x^2 - 2, 0, 2) @test x ≈ sqrt(2) atol = 1e-10 x, _ = bisection(x -> 1 - x, 0, 2) @test x ≈ 1 atol = 1e-10 end @testset "root at an endpoint" begin @test bisection(x -> x, 0.0, 1.0)[1] == 0.0 @test bisection(x -> x - 1, 0.0, 1.0)[1] == 1.0 end @testset "invalid inputs" begin @test_throws ArgumentError bisection(x -> x^2 + 1, 0.0, 1.0) @test_throws ArgumentError bisection(x -> x, 1.0, -1.0) end end; ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Test Summary: | Pass Total Time bisection | 7 7 0.1s ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Exercise 4: Some tests are missing The following function gives the honours associated with an exam grade: ```julia """ honours(grade) Return the honours associated with a `grade`. - Precondition: `0 ≤ grade ≤ 20`. - Postcondition: returns - `"Excellent"` if `grade ≥ 16`, - `"Very good"` if `14 ≤ grade < 16`, - `"Good"` if `12 ≤ grade < 14`, - `"Pass"` if `10 ≤ grade < 12`, - `"Fail"` if `grade < 10`. - Throws a `DomainError` if the precondition is not satisfied. """ function honours(grade::Real) if grade < 0 throw(DomainError(grade, "grade must be in [0, 20]")) end if grade >= 16 return "Excellent" elseif grade > 14 return "Very good" elseif grade >= 12 return "Good" elseif grade >= 10 return "Pass" else return "Fail" end end ``` A colleague has started to write the tests, and they all pass: ```julia @testset "honours" begin @test honours(17) == "Excellent" @test honours(11) == "Pass" @test honours(5) == "Fail" end ``` 1. These tests are not sufficient: list the items of the contract which are **not** checked. 2. Complete the test set. Remember to test the values **exactly at the boundaries**. 3. Your new tests should reveal two bugs: fix the function. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon=false} ## Hint for Exercise 4 There are five honours and two kinds of invalid grades (too small and too large). For each threshold $s \in \{10, 12, 14, 16\}$, test the grade $s$ itself. ::: ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" icon=false} ## Correction of Exercise 4 The first test set checks neither `"Very good"`, nor `"Good"`, nor any boundary, nor the invalid grades. The corrected function: ::: {#bf41f9a1 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function honours(grade::Real) if grade < 0 || grade > 20 # bug 1: grade > 20 was accepted throw(DomainError(grade, "grade must be in [0, 20]")) end if grade >= 16 return "Excellent" elseif grade >= 14 # bug 2: it was grade > 14 return "Very good" elseif grade >= 12 return "Good" elseif grade >= 10 return "Pass" else return "Fail" end end @testset "honours" begin @testset "one grade per honours" begin @test honours(17) == "Excellent" @test honours(15) == "Very good" @test honours(13) == "Good" @test honours(11) == "Pass" @test honours(5) == "Fail" end @testset "boundaries" begin @test honours(20) == "Excellent" @test honours(16) == "Excellent" @test honours(15.99) == "Very good" @test honours(14) == "Very good" @test honours(12) == "Good" @test honours(10) == "Pass" @test honours(9.99) == "Fail" @test honours(0) == "Fail" end @testset "invalid grades" begin @test_throws DomainError honours(-1) @test_throws DomainError honours(20.5) end end; ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Test Summary: | Pass Total Time honours | 15 15 0.0s ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon=false} ## To go further: what does the coverage say? Create a package `Grades` (see [Organising tests in a package](#organising-tests-in-a-package)) containing the **initial** (buggy) function `honours`, with the **initial** tests of your colleague in `test/runtests.jl`. Run the coverage with `LocalCoverage`. 1. Which lines are not covered? Are the bugs on these lines? 2. One of the two bugs cannot be detected by the coverage, even in theory. Which one, and why? **Answer.** The lines returning `"Very good"`, `"Good"` and throwing the `DomainError` are never executed: the coverage invites you to write tests for them. Testing `"Very good"` at the boundary `14` reveals the bug `grade > 14`. However, the missing condition `grade > 20` is *absent* from the code: there is no line to cover. Only the contract tells us that this case must be tested. This is why tests are written from the **contract**, and coverage is only used to check that no part of the code has been forgotten. :::
